bookinfo.title: Templatized C++ Command Line Parser Manual (v2.0)

sect1.title: Overview
sect1.para: This manual describes TCLAP 2.0, which is not source compatible with the 1.4/1.6 branches: every argument is now constructed with a single named-field aggregate instead of a list of positional constructor parameters, and an argument is never self-registered with a CmdLine from inside its own constructor. If you're maintaining code written against 1.4 or 1.6, keep an eye out for the notes throughout this manual that call out where 2.0 differs, or use the 1.4 (C++98) or 1.6 (same API, modernized internals) branches instead if you don't want these changes.

TCLAP has a few key classes to be aware of. The first is the CmdLine (command line) class. This class parses the command line passed to it according to the arguments that it contains. Arguments are separate objects that are added to the CmdLine object one at a time. The six argument classes are: ValueArg, UnlabeledValueArg, SwitchArg, MultiSwitchArg, MultiArg and UnlabeledMultiArg. These classes are templatized, which means they can be defined to parse a value of any type. Once you add the arguments to the CmdLine object, it parses the command line and assigns the data it finds to the specific argument objects it contains. Your program accesses the values parsed by calls to the value() methods of the argument objects.

sect1.title: Example
sect1.para: Here is a simple example ... Each argument is constructed by passing its constructor a single aggregate of named fields -- a C++20 designated initializer, e.g. {.flag = "n", .name = "name", ...} -- rather than the long, order-sensitive list of positional parameters used before 2.0. Every argument must then be added to the CmdLine with an explicit call to add(): 2.0 removed the constructor overloads that added an argument to a CmdLine passed in as a constructor parameter (see this note if you're migrating code that relied on that).

C++20 designated initializers must follow the fields' declaration order in that specific Spec. You may skip fields that have defaults, but you cannot reorder the fields you provide. For ValueArgSpec<T>, .required precedes .defaultValue, which precedes .typeDesc and .constraint. For example:

Placing .defaultValue after .typeDesc is ill-formed. The Spec types remain aggregates; this rule comes from C++20. Argument .name is mandatory even when other fields are omitted. Check the corresponding declaration rather than assuming every Spec has the same order: CmdLineSpec, SwitchArgSpec, MultiSwitchArgSpec, ValueArgSpec, MultiArgSpec, UnlabeledValueArgSpec, and UnlabeledMultiArgSpec.

sect2.title: Library Properties
sect2.para:
This example shows a number of different properties of the library...
Arguments can appear in any order (...mostly, more on this later).
The help, version and -- SwitchArgs are specified automatically. Using either the -h or --help flag will cause the USAGE message to be displayed, --version will cause any version information to be displayed (unlike the other automatic switches, it has no short flag by default, so it doesn't collide with a real -v your program might want), and -- or --ignore_rest will cause the remaining labeled arguments to be ignored. These switches are included by default on every command line. You can disable this functionality if desired (although we don't recommend it).
If there is an error parsing the command line (e.g. a required argument isn't provided), the program exits and displays a brief USAGE and an error message.
The program name is assumed to always be argv[0], so it isn't specified directly.
A value delimiter character can be specified via the Dialect passed to CmdLine (see below). This means that if you prefer arguments of the style -s=asdf instead of -s asdf, you can do so.
A malformed command line (a missing required argument, an unrecognized flag, a value that fails its type conversion or constraint) no longer throws in 2.0 -- see the note about parseOrExit() above. What still throws is constructing the CmdLine or an Arg with a malformed spec (a duplicate flag/name, a blank .name, and the like): that always throws a SpecificationException, uncaught, and is never turned into a ParseOutcome. When every Arg is constructed with a fixed, hardcoded spec -- as in every example in this manual -- that exception can only fire as a result of a bug in your code, so letting it propagate and crash the program during development is normally the right thing to do, the same way you'd want any other precondition violation to surface. If your specs are instead built from something runtime-determined (a config file, a plugin registering its own options), that assumption stops holding and you should catch SpecificationException yourself -- see the warning in the Example section.

sect2.title: Common Argument Properties
sect2.para:
Arguments, whatever their type, have a few common properties. These properties are set as named fields (.field = value) in the single designated-initializer aggregate passed to each argument's constructor -- ValueArgSpec<T> for ValueArg<T>, SwitchArgSpec for SwitchArg, and so on for every argument type. You can write the spec type name out explicitly (ValueArg<T>(ValueArgSpec<T>{...})), but it's almost always safe to just write ValueArg<T>({...}) instead -- the braced list is enough for the compiler to pick the right constructor, so naming the spec type again is redundant. See test1.cpp, above, for an example.
First is the flag (.flag), the character preceded by a dash(-) that signals the beginning of the argument on the command line.
Arguments also have a name (.name), which can also be used as an alternative flag on the command line, this time preceded by two dashes (--) [like the familiar getopt_long()]. Unlike every other field, .name is mandatory: leaving it out of the {...} list is a compile error rather than silently producing a blank name.
Next is the description (.description) of the argument. This is a short description of the argument displayed in the help/usage message when needed.
The remaining fields vary depending on the type of argument. Some possible ones include:
A boolean value (.required) indicating whether the Arg is required or not. A default value (.defaultValue). A description of the type of value expected (.typeDesc). A constraint on the value expected (.constraint).
No field takes the CmdLine to register the Arg with -- 2.0 removed the self-registering constructors that existed for this in earlier versions. Always call cmd.add(arg) explicitly after constructing the Arg; see below if you're migrating code that relied on the old behavior. See the API Documentation for more detail.

sect1.title: Explicitly empty values
sect1.para: An attached delimiter can carry an empty value, for example --name= when the parser delimiter is =. With the default space delimiter, pass an empty argv element (for example, --name "" in a shell). Strings and types with StringLike traits receive the empty string directly. Numeric values reject empty input. Custom stream extractors decide whether empty input is valid through their operator>> implementation; no default-value substitution is performed. Constraints still check explicitly supplied values, including empty strings. These rules apply to both ValueArg and MultiArg. Omitting a value entirely is still an error.

sect1.title: Argument prefixes
sect1.para: Set CmdLineSpec::dialect to select parsing conventions for a parser. Dialect::flagPrefix is a string containing exactly one character, such as - or /. Empty or multiple-character short prefixes are rejected with a SpecificationException before automatic arguments are constructed, even when help/version is disabled. Dialect::namePrefix may contain multiple characters, such as --. Combined short switches use the single short-prefix character.

sect1.title: Compiling
sect1.para: For installed CMake consumers, use find_package(TCLAP CONFIG REQUIRED) and link your application target with target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE TCLAP::TCLAP). Use CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH for a custom installation prefix, or TCLAP_DIR for a nonstandard package metadata directory. See INSTALL in the source root for a complete example. The imported target propagates the C++20 language requirement.

TCLAP is implemented entirely in header files which means you only need to include CmdLine.h to use the library.
#include <tclap/CmdLine.h>
You'll need to make sure that your compiler can see the header files. If you do the usual "make install" then your compiler should see the files by default. Alternatively, you can use the -I complier argument to specify the exact location of the libraries.
c++ -std=c++20 -o my_program -I /some/place/tclap-2.X/include my_program.cpp
Where /some/place/tclap-2.X is the place you have unpacked the distribution.

Finally, if you want to include TCLAP as part of your software (which is perfectly OK, even encouraged) then simply copy the contents of /some/place/tclap-2.X/include (the tclap directory and all of the header files it contains) into your include directory.

TCLAP 2.0 requires a C++20 compiler and a C++20 standard library that provides std::format. It uses C++20 features, including designated initializers and concepts, throughout its public API and implementation. This is unlike the 1.4 branch, which stays on C++98 for maximum portability, and unlike 1.6, which is also a C++20 rewrite of TCLAP's internals but keeps 1.4's original, source-compatible API rather than the one this manual describes. If your project needs a C++98-compatible TCLAP, or you want 2.0's modernized internals without the API changes this manual describes, use the 1.4 or 1.6 branch instead. Please let us know if your C++20 compiler doesn't work with 2.0!

The CmdLine class contains the arguments that define the command line and manages the parsing of the command line. The CmdLine doesn't parse the command line itself it only manages the parsing. The actual parsing of individual arguments occurs within the arguments themselves. The CmdLine keeps track of of the required arguments, relationships between arguments, and output generation.

SwitchArgs are what the name implies: simple, on/off, boolean switches. Use SwitchArgs anytime you want to turn some sort of system property on or off. SwitchArgs don't parse a value. They return TRUE or FALSE, depending on whether the switch has been found on the command line and what the default value was defined as.

ValueArgs are arguments that read a value of some type from the command line. Any time you need a file name, a number, etc. use a ValueArg or one of its variants. All ValueArgs are templatized and will attempt to parse the string its flag matches on the command line as the type it is specified as. ValueArg<int> will attempt to parse an int, ValueArg<float> will attempt to parse a float, etc. If operator>> for the specified type doesn't recognize the string on the command line as its defined type, that's a command-line parsing error like any other -- reported via the ParseOutcome that parse() returns (see the note about parseOrExit() above), not an exception.
A MultiArg is a ValueArg that can be specified more than once on a command line and instead of returning a single value, returns a vector of values.
Imagine a compiler that allows you to specify multiple directories to search for libraries...
An UnlabeledValueArg is a ValueArg that is not identified by a flag on the command line. Instead UnlabeledValueArgs are identified by their position in the argv array.

An UnlabeledMultiArg is an UnlabeledValueArg that allows more than one value to be specified. Only one UnlabeledMultiArg can be specified per command line. The UnlabeledMultiArg simply reads the remaining unmatched operand values through the end of argv, including values after -- with its normal non-ignoreable setting. The marker itself is consumed by the parser. See end option recognition for the ignoreable policy and branch-specific limitations.

chapter.title: Complications
chapter.para: Naturally, what we have seen to this point doesn't satisfy all of our needs.

sect1.title: I want to combine multiple switches into one argument...
sect1.para:
Multiple SwitchArgs can be combined into a single argument on the command line. If you have switches -a, -b and -c it is valid to do either:
% command -a -b -c
or
% command -abc
or
% command -ba -c
This is to make this library more in line with the POSIX and GNU standards (as I understand them).

sect1.title: I want one argument or the other, but not both...
sect1.para:
Suppose you have a command that must read input from one of two possible locations, either a local file or a URL. The command must read something, so one argument is required, but not both, yet neither argument is strictly necessary by itself.
TCLAP can automatically enforce such constraints on a set of arguments using an argument group of type OneOf.

AnyOf groups arguments for presentation only. It does not require a member to be selected or make one member depend on another. Each argument's own requirements still apply; check any conditional dependencies in application code after a successful parse.

sect1.title: ...but I don't want to require either one
sect1.para: There is also the class EitherOf that works the same way, except it does not require any argument to be set. This can be useful if there is a natural default. For example, selecting the encryption algorithm may default to AES, but there may be flags for choosing another algorithm and they are all mutually exclusive.

sect1.title: I have more arguments than single flags make sense for...
Parse failures and reuse
sect1.para: Check the result of the entire parse before using any argument values for application work. Parsing is not transactional: an error may leave earlier arguments changed, or even store a value that subsequently fails its constraint. isSet() does not restore old values and cannot substitute for checking the whole parse.

To parse again, call reset() and supply fresh input. The vector overload expects the program name at element 0 and erases that element. Reset restores parser/argument state, not the caller's input vector.

With parse(), continue only for Outcome::Success. HelpRequested, VersionRequested and ParseError all stop normal application work; reporting has already occurred. Malformed specifications and exceptions from custom callbacks/output/extractors can still throw. parseOrExit() is an alternative for a CLI main that should exit on help, version or errors.

add() borrows its argument; it does not copy it or transfer ownership. Keep caller-owned arguments alive while the parser uses them. Constraints and custom output objects passed to setOutput() are also borrowed and must remain alive while used. Declare dependencies before the objects that refer to them. This example declares the constraint and output first, the argument next, and the parser last, so destruction happens in the reverse order:

Groups passed to add() are borrowed too. Use separate argument and group objects for separate live parsers. Callbacks are stored by value, but any object captured by reference must remain alive when the callback runs. addOwned<ArgType>() owns only the argument it constructs; it does not take ownership of that argument's constraint or of referenced callback captures. Keep the parser alive while using its owned argument references and registered arguments' dialect.

sect1.title: I want to constrain the values allowed for a particular argument...
sect1.para: Constraints check values explicitly supplied on the command line. An omitted optional argument has isSet() equal to false, and its default value is intentionally not checked against its constraint. The application decides whether and how to use that default. For example, an optional integer may default to 0 even if its allowed input values are 1 and 2. A required argument must still be supplied: its default does not satisfy the requirement. Read values only after the whole parse succeeds.

For example, one might wish to allow only integers greater than 0. In this case, simply create a class that implements the Constraint<int> interface and checks whether the value parsed is greater than 0 (done in the check() method) and set the .constraint field of your Arg's spec to point at your new Constraint.
TCLAP provides a simple way to constrain the allowed values to a list of values. Simply create a ValuesConstraint object with a vector of values and set it as the Arg's .constraint.

sect1.title: Why do I have to call cmd.add() myself now?
I want different output than what is provided...
sect1.para: The example above reads argument metadata through ArgModel/ArgGroupModel (ArgModel.h) rather than through Arg/ArgGroup directly -- this is the recommended starting point for a custom CmdLineOutput that doesn't need to distinguish exclusive argument groups in its rendering (see the section on argument groups). BuildArgGroupModels() returns one ArgGroupModel per registered ArgGroup -- including the CmdLine's own built-in groups for plainly add()'d arguments and for the auto-added --help/--version/ -- switches -- each holding an ArgModel per member with plain-data fields (flag, name, description, shortID, longID, and the like) instead of requiring you to call into Arg's virtual interface. A consumer that doesn't care about grouping at all, like the example above, can just iterate every group's members in a nested loop, as shown.

If you need output that distinguishes exclusive groups the way StdOutput's own usage() does -- rendering an EitherOf/ OneOf group as {a|b} rather than listing its members individually -- use ArgGroupModel's isExclusive/ isRequired/showAsGroup fields to detect and render that case specially; see StdOutput.h's own _shortUsage() for the reference implementation of that logic (it reads directly from CmdLineInterface::argList()/ argGroups(), the same lower-level accessors ArgGroupModel itself is built from, still available directly if you need something ArgGroupModel doesn't expose).

sect1.title: I don't want the --help and --version switches to be created automatically...
sect1.para:
Help and version information is useful for nearly all command line applications and as such we generate flags that provide those options automatically. However, there are situations when these flags are undesirable. For these cases the CmdLine spec has a .helpAndVersion field. Setting it to false will disable automatic help and version generation.
CmdLine cmd({.message = "this is a message", .version = "0.99", .helpAndVersion = false});

sect1.title: End option recognition with --
sect1.para: The automatically registered -- marker ends option recognition. POSIX/GNU conventions treat following tokens as operands, including tokens beginning with a dash; they do not mean that all following input is discarded. TCLAP's ordinary unlabeled arguments consume those tokens in their registered order. The marker itself is not an operand.

For example, with a switch -x and an unlabeled multi argument for files, prog -x before -- -x after sets the switch once and supplies the three operands before, -x and after. The second -x is a file name, not another switch occurrence. Required arguments are still checked after --; the marker does not satisfy missing requirements.

TCLAP implements this through its separate ignoreable policy. Labeled arguments are normally ignoreable, so they stop matching after the marker. Unmatched remaining tokens are not reported as unknown-option errors. Unlabeled arguments are normally not ignoreable and therefore continue consuming input. Setting an unlabeled argument's .ignoreable = true makes it stop consuming after the marker as well. This is a TCLAP policy choice, separate from the standard meaning of ending option recognition.

sect1.title: I want to ignore unmatched arguments...
sect1.para: NOTE: If both ignoreUnmatched is set to true and an UnlabeledMultiArg is added to the command line, then the UnlabeledMultiArg will "win" and all extra arguments will be added to it rather than be ignored.

sect1.title: I want to read hex integers as arguments...
sect1.para: Unlike the pre-2.0 TCLAP_SETBASE_ZERO compile-time macro this replaces (which applied to every integer ValueArg/MultiArg in the whole program at once, whether you wanted it there or not), AutoBaseInt<T> is an explicit, per-Arg opt-in: auto-base and decimal-only integer Args can coexist in the same program. AutoBaseInt<T> converts implicitly to T, so _intTest above could just as well have been declared AutoBaseInt<int> directly instead of int.

sect1.title: Numeric syntax and migration from 1.x
sect1.para: Ordinary integer and floating-point types use std::from_chars in 2.0. Signed integers accept 7 and -7; unsigned integers reject negative input. A leading plus such as +7 is rejected for both ordinary integers and floating-point values, whereas 1.x stream-based parsing accepts it. Leading whitespace is accepted, but trailing whitespace or any other unconsumed characters are rejected. Trailing whitespace rejection also applies in 1.x; it is not a migration change.

Ordinary integers are decimal: 010 means 10 and 0x10 is rejected. Floating-point input accepts decimal and exponent forms such as 1.5 and 1e3, as well as inf, -inf and nan. Parsing those spellings does not bypass constraints: for example, a finite RangeConstraint rejects infinities and NaN. The numeric conversion is independent of the stream locale: the decimal point is ., and 1,5 is rejected even with a comma locale. Leading-whitespace classification uses the current C character locale.

bool, plain char and custom ValueLike types use stream extraction instead. With the default stream locale, bool accepts 0/1, not true/false; char reads a character such as x, not its numeric code. Streams use their locale and custom extractors determine their own syntax. StringLike types use assignment and preserve spaces rather than numeric conversion.

Use AutoBaseInt<int> explicitly to choose stream-based C-style bases for one argument: 0x10 is 16, 010 is 8, and 10 is 10. This wrapper accepts +7 and -7; invalid octal 08 and trailing whitespace are rejected. See the auto-base example.

sect1.title: I want to use different types...
sect1.para: Custom value types must satisfy Parseable<T> in ValueParsing.h: they must be std::default_initializable and support the applicable parsing category. Every parse creates a fresh T{}; supplying an explicit .defaultValue does not remove that requirement.

Ordinary arithmetic types use std::from_chars, except bool and plain char that use stream extraction. Wide/UTF character types do not automatically satisfy Parseable. A custom ValueLike type needs operator>>(std::istream&, T&). A StringLike type is selected by an ArgTraits<T> specialization or T::ValueCategory (including inheritance from StringLikeTrait) and must support SetString, normally assignment from std::string. Selecting that category alone does not implement assignment. See numeric syntax for the conversion paths. Stream output is needed when printing values or using ValuesConstraint; an output operator alone does not make a type parseable.

Storage adds requirements beyond the parsing concept. Parsed values must be constructible from an rvalue for the result and storage paths. ValueArg<T> copies the initial default into its current value, stores another default, assigns the parsed value, and copy-assigns the stored default during reset. It therefore needs copying and assignment as well as parsing; arbitrary move-only types do not work there. MultiArg<T> stores results in std::vector<T> and clears that vector on reset; its element type must support insertion and relocation. A suitable move-only type can work with MultiArg even though it cannot work with ValueArg. Constraints and application operations may impose further requirements. The pair example below supplies default construction, copying, assignment and stream input.
